regions.label: The tiers of the audience
regions.text: Behind the performers the audience rises in strict horizontal tiers, graded by the price of the seats. Top hats and gloves fill the rows nearest the ring; caps and leaning elbows crowd the gallery above. Seurat drew them with a caricaturist's economy — a dot, a curve, a dark oval — and set them in rigid horizontals so that the curved, rising lines of the performance below read as the opposite of ordinary life.

regions.label: The bareback rider
regions.text: The rider balances on one slipper on the back of a cantering white horse, arms open, skirt flaring like a struck match. Everything about her obeys the theory: lines that rise from the horizontal signify gaiety, and warm colour — orange above all — carries joy. She is the point at which Seurat's system, built by measurement over years of patient work, is asked to manufacture delight itself.

regions.label: The clown in the foreground
regions.text: A clown in red stands with his back to us, holding the curtain aside. He puts the viewer in the cheap standing room at the edge of the ring, watching the show over a stranger's shoulder. It is the picture's sharpest formal invention: the largest figure on the canvas is the one whose face we never see, and his dark silhouette closes the composition like a hand cupped around a flame.
